div.head: Leis Wl 15
div.ab: E si aucuns est apeled de mustier fruissir u de chambre, e il n’ait esté en ariere blasmé, s’en escundisse par XIIII humes leals numez sei duzime main.
E si alcons est apelez de muster fruisser u de chambre, e il n’eit ested blamed en arere, s’en escondie per X[II]II leals homes nomez sei dudzime main.

Si appellatur quis de uiolatione ecclesie uel camere. Si quis appellatur, quod aut ecclesie immunitatem aut alicuius cameram infregerit, si hactenus de tali crimine immunis fuerit et inculpabilis, purget se iuramento per XIIII legales homines nominatos manu duodecima.
E si aucuns est apeled de mustier fruissir u de chambre, e il n'ait esté en ariere blasmé, s'en escundisse par XIIII humes leals numez sei duzime main.
15. Und wenn jemand Kirche oder Kammer erbrochen zu [haben] angeklagt ist und er bisher nicht bescholten worden ist, so reinige er sich davon durch 14 ernannte gesetzmässige Männer selbzwölfter Hand.

15. And if someone is accused of [having] broken into a church or chamber and he has not hitherto been ill-reputed, then he shall clear himself of it by 14 nominated lawful men, with himself as twelfth hand.

And if anyone is accused of breaking into a church or a treasury, and has no previous convictions against him, he shall clear himself of the charge with 11 compurgators found among 14 qualified men nominated [by the court].

‘Kloster’ zu eng Riley; die weitere Bed. bezeugen Godefroy, La Curne.—Dagegen in hierarchischer Absicht zu weit L wie o. 1
‘Monastery’ (Riley) is too narrow; the wider meaning is attested by Godefroy and La Curne.—L, on the other hand, is too wide, with hierarchical intent, as above 1

‘Wohnraum’ (La Curne, nicht allgemein ‘Haus’), bes. ‘Schatzkammer’ (Ducange), also wohl (wie Phillips Engl. RG. I 192 meint) des Königs oder Klosters. Die Königskammer, auch Schlafgemach, war zugleich Schatz im 11./12. Jh.; Tout Place of Edward II. p. 44. 63. Vgl. Gl Schatz 2; Einbruch 6ff. [In Wardrobe-Schatz zu Westminster ward 1303 eingebrochen.] Dagegen denkt L an die Kammer irgend jemands. S. o. 14, 1

‘Living-room’ (La Curne; not ‘house’ in general), esp. ‘treasure-chamber’ (Ducange), and so probably (as Phillips Engl. RG. I 192 thinks) the king’s or a monastery’s. The king’s chamber, which was also his bedchamber, was at the same time the treasury in the 11th/12th cent.; Tout Place of Edward II. p. 44. 63. Cf. Gl Schatz 2; Einbruch 6ff. [The Wardrobe treasury at Westminster was broken into in 1303.] L, on the other hand, thinks of anybody’s chamber. See above 14, 1
